IA-FC-01: A reconciliation is how you prove a balance is real. Done badly, errors and theft sit undisturbed for years.
IA-FC-02: When the close is rushed to hit a deadline, the checks are the first thing dropped.
IA-FC-03: Estimates are the numbers management gets to choose. That is exactly why they need challenging.
IA-FC-04: Group accounts are built by combining many companies. If balances between them do not cancel out, the group figures are wrong.
IA-FC-05: Using the wrong exchange rate quietly changes profit, and it is very hard to spot from the outside.
IA-FC-06: The notes in the accounts are part of the accounts. Getting them wrong is a reporting failure, not a formatting one.
IA-FC-07: If accounts in the ledger can be changed freely, the reports built on them stop meaning what people think.
IA-FC-08: Deals with people connected to the business must be disclosed. Hiding them is where governance scandals usually start.
IA-FC-09: The board makes decisions from these reports. If the numbers cannot be traced back to the ledger, the decisions rest on nothing.
IA-FA-01: Capital spending is committed years in advance and is very hard to reverse once started.
IA-FA-02: If an asset is on the register but nobody can find it, either it was stolen or the records are wrong. Both matter.
IA-FA-03: Calling a repair an asset spreads the cost over years and makes this year's profit look better than it is.
IA-FA-04: Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its life. Wrong life, wrong profit, every single year.
IA-FA-05: Selling company assets cheaply to someone you know is one of the oldest frauds there is.
IA-FA-06: When an asset stops earning its keep, the loss has already happened. Recognising it late just delays bad news.
IA-FA-07: Projects left as 'under construction' avoid depreciation, so finished assets sometimes stay there on purpose.
IA-FA-08: Rented assets now sit on the balance sheet. Leases nobody has identified mean the balance sheet is incomplete.
IA-FA-09: Uninsured or badly maintained assets turn a single bad day into a very expensive one.
IA-TX-01: Without someone clearly owning tax risk, positions get taken across the group that nobody has assessed together.
IA-TX-02: Corporate tax filed late or wrongly attracts interest and penalties, and authorities can look back several years.
IA-TX-03: Sales tax and VAT are applied to enormous numbers of transactions, so a small error repeated becomes a large bill.
IA-TX-04: Treating someone as a contractor when they work like an employee creates back-tax liabilities plus penalties.
IA-TX-05: When group companies charge each other, tax authorities want proof the price was fair. No proof means an adjustment.
IA-TX-06: The tax numbers in the accounts are estimates too, and they depend on forecasts that may not hold.
IA-TX-07: When a tax authority finds something, the same issue usually exists elsewhere in the group.
IA-TX-08: Tax is often calculated in spreadsheets nobody controls, which makes errors invisible until an authority finds them.
IA-HR-01: Headcount is one of the largest costs a business has, and it grows quietly when nobody enforces the approved plan.
IA-HR-02: Hiring without a fair, documented process invites both bad hires and discrimination claims.
IA-HR-03: In regulated or safety-critical roles, an expired certificate means the person should not be doing the job at all.
IA-HR-04: Handling grievances inconsistently is how employment claims and tribunal costs are created.
IA-HR-05: Unexplained pay differences between people doing the same job are a legal exposure and a retention problem.
IA-HR-06: Employee records contain some of the most sensitive data a company holds, including health information.
IA-HR-07: If only one person knows how something critical works, their resignation is an operational incident.
IA-INV-01: If what arrives is not properly checked and recorded, every stock figure after that point is already wrong.
IA-INV-02: Stock sitting in a warehouse is portable and saleable, which is why custody controls matter more than they look.
IA-INV-03: Counting stock is how you find out what is really there. Letting the same people count their own stock defeats the point.
IA-INV-04: The cost attached to each item decides both the stock value and the reported margin on every sale.
IA-INV-05: Stock that will never sell at full price is worth less than the books say, and saying so is uncomfortable.
IA-INV-06: Stock held elsewhere, or in transit, is easy to count twice or not at all.
IA-INV-07: Scrap and returns are a legitimate-looking route for stock to leave the building.
IA-IT-01: Most major system outages are caused by a change someone made, not by an attacker.
IA-IT-02: Overnight processing runs the business. When a job fails silently, the numbers are simply incomplete.
IA-IT-03: Attackers use known weaknesses that already have fixes available. Unpatched systems are an open door.
IA-IT-04: Most breaches start with a person clicking something or a password being reused, not with sophisticated hacking.
IA-IT-05: Having backups is not the same as being able to restore. You find out which you have on the worst day.
IA-IT-06: Using a cloud provider moves the work, not the accountability. If it goes down, your business goes down.
IA-IT-07: Data that nobody owns gets kept too long, shared too widely, and eventually leaked.
IA-IT-08: Untracked laptops walk out of the door, and unlicensed software invites an expensive audit from the vendor.
IA-IT-09: Large technology projects fail slowly and quietly, and status reports stay green until the day they do not.
IA-IT-10: A surprising amount of financial reporting depends on a spreadsheet on one person's drive with no version control.
IA-IT-11: Old systems that nobody wants to touch keep running until the day they cannot be fixed any more.
IA-O2C-01: Fake or duplicated customer records are how fictitious sales and diverted refunds are set up.
IA-O2C-02: Giving credit to someone who cannot pay is a decision to lose money, taken one order at a time.
IA-O2C-03: Accepting an order commits the business to terms it may not be able to meet.
IA-O2C-04: Discounts and rebates are given away one transaction at a time and rarely reviewed in total.
IA-O2C-05: Recording a delivery in the wrong period moves profit between years, which is a classic way to flatter results.
IA-O2C-06: Goods delivered but never invoiced is money the business has simply given away.
IA-O2C-07: Credit notes reverse sales. They are also the easiest way to hide a debt that was never going to be collected.
IA-O2C-08: Money received but not matched to an invoice makes the debt look overdue and hides where cash actually went.
IA-O2C-09: The longer a debt goes unchased, the less of it comes back.
IA-O2C-10: Not providing for debts that will never be paid overstates both profit and what the business is owed.
IA-O2C-11: When revenue is recognised is a judgement, and judgements around year end get pressure applied to them.
IA-P2P-01: Set up a fake supplier, or change a real one's bank details, and payments walk straight out of the company.
IA-P2P-02: Awarding work without competition costs money, and is often where undisclosed personal interests hide.
IA-P2P-03: An approved order is the point at which the company becomes committed to spend. After that it is too late.
IA-P2P-04: Confirming that goods or services arrived is what stops the company paying for nothing, and it is hardest to prove for services.
IA-P2P-05: Matching the invoice to the order and the delivery is the basic check that stops overbilling.
IA-P2P-06: This is the moment cash actually leaves. Everything before it is preparation.
IA-P2P-07: Paying the same invoice twice is common, rarely noticed, and usually only recovered if someone looks.
IA-P2P-08: Expenses and company cards are small amounts approved quickly, which is exactly why personal spending slips through.
IA-P2P-09: Companies negotiate good rates and then pay something different, because nobody checks the invoice against the contract.
IA-P2P-10: Buyers control who gets the business, which makes them a target for suppliers offering something on the side.
IA-P2P-11: Leaving out bills that have already been incurred makes profit look better than it is.
IA-PAY-01: If one person can add an employee, set their pay and release the payment, nothing stops them paying themselves.
IA-PAY-02: Changing bank details or salary is the quickest way to redirect or inflate pay.
IA-PAY-03: Someone independent looking at the payroll before it goes out is the last chance to catch anything wrong.
IA-PAY-04: People get paid for the hours recorded, so whoever controls the hours controls the cost.
IA-PAY-05: Overtime and bonuses are the variable part of pay, which makes them the part worth claiming falsely.
IA-PAY-06: Tax and social security deducted from staff belongs to the authorities. Paying it late brings penalties immediately.
IA-PAY-07: People get paid after they leave more often than anyone expects, and it is rarely recovered.
IA-PAY-08: Unused holiday and long-service benefits are a real liability that builds quietly on the balance sheet.
IA-PAY-09: The file sent to the bank is what actually pays people. It must match what was approved.
IA-PAY-10: Using a payroll provider does not transfer the responsibility. If they get it wrong, your staff are unpaid.
IA-PAY-11: Comparing payroll to HR records is how you find people being paid who do not exist.
IA-TP-01: You cannot manage suppliers you do not know you have, and most companies have more than they think.
IA-TP-02: Checking a supplier after you depend on them is too late to do anything about what you find.
IA-TP-03: The contract is the only leverage you have when a supplier fails. Missing terms means no remedy.
IA-TP-04: If nobody measures the service, it drifts, and the credits you were owed are never claimed.
IA-TP-05: When a supplier performs a control for you, you still have to prove it works.
IA-TP-06: A data breach at your supplier is reported as your data breach.
IA-TP-07: If a critical supplier fails and there is no alternative, the disruption lasts as long as it lasts.
IA-TP-08: Moving work to another country brings regulatory, tax and oversight issues that are easy to miss.
IA-EL-01: The board is the last line of defence. If it cannot see problems or will not challenge, nothing else compensates.
IA-EL-02: People take their cue from what leaders reward and tolerate, not from what the policy says.
IA-EL-03: If the risk register does not contain the things that actually go wrong, risk management is decoration.
IA-EL-04: A policy nobody knows about or follows provides no protection, only the appearance of it.
IA-EL-05: If it is unclear who can approve what, decisions get made by people without the authority to make them.
IA-EL-06: Fraud does not get prevented by general controls. Someone has to think specifically about how it would be done here.
IA-EL-07: If raising a concern feels unsafe, management finds out about problems from the regulator or the press instead.
IA-EL-08: Regulatory obligations that nobody owns get missed, and being told by the regulator is the expensive way to find out.
IA-EL-09: Plans that have never been tested tend not to work when they are finally needed.
IA-TR-01: Running out of cash kills otherwise profitable businesses. The forecast is what stops that happening.
IA-TR-02: Loan agreements contain promises. Break one and the lender can demand its money back immediately.
IA-TR-03: Currency and interest rate moves can swing profit even when the business is performing exactly as planned.
IA-TR-04: Chasing slightly better returns with spare cash is how companies lose money they were not trying to risk.
IA-TR-05: Money moved between group companies without proper agreements creates tax and legal problems later.
IA-TR-06: Guarantees are promises to pay if someone else does not. They are easy to give and easy to forget.
IA-TR-07: If the same person can do a deal and settle it, money can move with no independent check at all.
IA-TR-08: Companies routinely have bank accounts nobody at head office knows about.
